unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: the biological definition of cancer as a genetic disease involving clonal evolution and microenvironmental support
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: the drivers of cancer mutations, the interplay between endogenous 'bad luck' and environmental exposures, and global epidemiological variations
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 2 establishes what cancer is biologically, whereas subtopic 3 opens a new core question regarding what drives mutation acquisition, introducing the 'roulette wheel' framework and initiating an extended discussion of endogenous versus environmental causation and epidemiology.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 2 and 3 can both be seen as introductory background laying the theoretical foundations of cancer mutation and development before examining specific carcinogens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: dietary carcinogens and the mechanism of aflatoxin-induced DNA adducts
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: UV radiation damage and thymine dimer formation
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 10 moves from chemical ingested mutagens to physical radiation-induced DNA damage.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 10 is a brief illustration within a continuous catalogue of direct mutagenic agents and mechanisms of DNA damage spanning subtopics 9 through 13.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: UV radiation damage and thymine dimer formation
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzo[a]pyrene and TCDD requiring xenobiotic activation to cause DNA damage
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 11 introduces a specific class of chemical mutagens in cigarette smoke and diet that require enzymatic metabolic activation via CYP1A1.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 11 simply continues the sequence of environmental mutagens and their molecular modes of DNA disruption.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: xenobiotic activation of benzo[a]pyrene and TCDD-induced oxidative stress
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: aromatic amines, beta-naphthylamine metabolism, and bladder-specific carcinogenicity
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 13 specifically addresses tissue-specific metabolic activation rather than general mutagenic activation.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 13 is the final specific example of direct/indirect chemical mutagens that complete the section on DNA-damaging carcinogens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: non-mutagenic tumor promoters, chronic inflammation (asbestos), and the Berenbaum two-stage model
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: host developmental stages, tissue proliferative states, alkylating agents (MNU), and a synthesis of carcinogenesis mechanisms
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 16 shifts from promoter/initiator signaling mechanisms to host-specific susceptibility factors such as puberty and reproductive timing.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 14 to 17 form a coherent broader inquiry into non-direct-mutagenic factors and host/environmental conditions that permit tumor development.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: identifying carcinogen exposure via genome sequencing and mutational signatures
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: using epidemiology, biomarkers, and population biobanks to prove carcinogenicity
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 19 transitions from molecular genomic profiling to population-level epidemiological studies and biobanks.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 18 through 21 all address the unified topic of methodologies and experimental models used to detect and prove carcinogenicity.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: epidemiology, urinary biomarkers, and biobank studies for determining carcinogenicity
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: in vivo animal toxicology models, species concordance, and dosage considerations
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 20 moves from observational human epidemiology to interventional animal toxicology testing.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 20 is just one of the testing methodologies surveyed in the broader topic on evaluating carcinogens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: in vivo animal toxicology models, species concordance, and dosage considerations
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: in vitro bacterial mutagenesis testing using the Ames test and its limitations
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 21 introduces in vitro laboratory screening assays as opposed to animal models.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 21 directly concludes the comparative overview of methods used to assess carcinogenic potential.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces the course structure, her background, and the learning objectives regarding cancer causation and carcinogen appraisal.

topics.label: Biological Nature of Cancer as an Evolutionary Disease
topics.groupedBecause: The subtopic defines cancer as a clonal, evolutionary genetic disease dependent on mutation accumulation and a supportive microenvironment.

topics.label: Etiology of Cancer: Endogenous Errors, Environmental Risks, and Epidemiology
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore what drives cancer mutations, contrasting endogenous 'bad luck' replication errors with environmental mutagens and supporting this with global epidemiological patterns.

topics.label: Infectious Pathogens in Cancer Etiology
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics discuss how bacterial, parasitic, and viral infections drive carcinogenesis, focusing on the mechanism and discovery of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Chemical and Physical Mutagens and Molecular Mechanisms of DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail specific dietary, radiation, and chemical mutagens and the molecular mechanisms by which they or their metabolic derivatives damage DNA.

topics.label: Tumor Promotion, Inflammation, and Host Developmental Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine non-mutagenic factors in cancer development, including tumor promoters, chronic inflammation, host life-stage susceptibility, and an overall mechanistic summary.

topics.label: Methodologies for Detecting and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the different experimental and observational approaches used to establish carcinogenicity, including mutational signature sequencing, epidemiology, biobanks, animal models, and the Ames test.

topics.label: Summary and Risk-Benefit Analysis
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer concludes the lecture by framing carcinogenic exposure as a practical risk-benefit analysis and summarizing the main takeaways.
